title: WMO promotes Earth's energy imbalance to a headline indicator, and we check it against our own arithmetic

blocks.text: The WMO published State of the Global Climate 2025 on 23 March 2026, on World Meteorological Day, under the theme Observing Today, Protecting Tomorrow. The coverage went to the quotable parts: the eleven hottest years, the emergency language from the UN Secretary-General, the cost of extreme weather. The structural change in the report went almost unremarked, and it is the change that matters most for anyone trying to read the climate system rather than the headlines.

One disclosure before the numbers. The full report PDF sits behind a slider check at library.wmo.int and would not download to an automated fetcher on 2026-08-09. Everything quoted below comes from the WMO press release that accompanies the report, which carries the report's own figures and its own key messages. Where a number is not in the press release we have not invented one.
THE NEW INDICATOR

WMO: 'For the first time, the report includes the Earth's energy imbalance as one of the key climate indicators.' Its key-message line reads 'Earth's energy imbalance is highest in sixty five-year record'. The imbalance has increased since its observational record began in 1960, particularly in the past 20 years, and reached a new high in 2025. Published 2026-03-23.

WMO gives the partition of the excess energy: more than 91 per cent is stored in the ocean, about 5 per cent in the continental land masses, about 3 per cent warms and melts ice, and the warming of the atmosphere including the near-surface temperatures that humans feel is just 1 per cent. Published 2026-03-23.

Our reading. That partition is why this promotion is worth recording. Global surface temperature, the number every January round is built around, is the thermometer reading on the 1 per cent, and it is the noisiest 1 per cent, because it is the part El Nino and La Nina swing hardest. Earth's energy imbalance is the term that says whether the planet is still gaining energy at all and at what rate, and it barely notices the Pacific. A record imbalance during a La Nina year is a specific combination that a surface-temperature-only reading cannot produce, and it is the combination WMO reported.
THE NUMBER, AND OUR OWN VERSION OF IT

WMO: ocean heat content to 2000 metres reached its highest level since records began in 1960, exceeding the previous high set in 2024, and each of the past nine years has set a new record. The rate of ocean warming over 2005-2025 is more than twice that over 1960-2005, and is about 11.0 to 12.2 Zettajoules per year, which WMO describes as about 18 times annual human energy use. Published 2026-03-23.

This project carries a derived energy imbalance series because no observed one is reachable without a key: CERES EBAF needs the LaRC ordering tool and the GCOS heat inventory sits behind a login. So we compute one, in the open, from the ocean heat content we do hold.

blocks.caption: OUR CALCULATION, NOT AN OBSERVATION. A 10-year trailing least-squares trend through NOAA's 0-2000 m ocean heat content, divided by the ocean's 0.89 share of the Earth heat inventory and by Earth's surface area.

blocks.text: Our reading, and it is arithmetic you can redo. The window ending 2025 gives 0.80 W/m2. Multiplied back out by the 0.89 ocean share, Earth's 5.1 x 10^14 m2 and the seconds in a year, that is an ocean uptake of 11.4 Zettajoules per year, which sits inside WMO's stated 11.0 to 12.2. Fitting a single straight line through the whole 2005-2025 NOAA record instead gives 10.83 Zettajoules per year, just under WMO's low end, which is the expected result for one product inside a range that spans several. Computed 2026-08-09 from the NOAA file this project already ingests.
That agreement is narrower than it looks, and the narrowness is the honest part. What agrees is the OCEAN term. Our number is not an energy imbalance measurement and should not be read as one.

Our reading of our own limits, all three stated on the chart itself. The input stops at 2000 metres, so the deep ocean below that is simply missing and biases the result low. The 0.89 ocean share is a 1971-2018 period average from von Schuckmann et al. 2020 applied to every year, and WMO's own report now says more than 91 per cent, which would push our number lower still. A trailing trend cannot see a turn until the window has passed over it. Published estimates anchored on CERES put recent imbalance nearer 0.9 to 1.0 W/m2, and the Indicators of Global Climate Change consortium gives 1.04 [0.82 to 1.25] W/m2 for the 2006-2025 mean. Our 0.80 sitting below that is this method behaving as designed, not a disagreement with the measurements.

The boring reading of the headline. A 65-year record beginning in 1960 is 66 annual values, and the half before Argo floats went global around 2005 rests on sampling far sparser than the half after. 'Highest in the record' is a true statement about a real record, but it is a short record whose early part is thin, and a series that climbs steadily will keep producing new highs without any of them being a distinct physical event. The claim in the report that carries more weight is the one about the rate: ocean warming over 2005-2025 more than double 1960-2005. A doubling of a rate across two multi-decade blocks survives sampling noise in a way that one annual maximum does not.

A second boring reading, on the timing. 2025 was a La Nina year, and La Nina is the phase in which the Pacific buries heat in the subsurface ocean instead of venting it to the atmosphere. Some part of a record ocean heat content and a record imbalance in exactly that year is redistribution within the system rather than extra energy arriving at the top of the atmosphere. This does not explain the multi-decade trend, and WMO does not claim it does, but it is the right caution before treating a single La Nina year's record as a step change.
WHAT ELSE THE REPORT LEADS WITH

Temperature: the annually averaged global near-surface temperature in 2025 was about 1.43 plus or minus 0.13 C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average, the second or third warmest year depending on the dataset, in a 176-year observational record. 2015-2025 were the eleven warmest years on record. 2024 remains the warmest at about 1.55 C. WMO attributes the step down from 2024 to the shift to La Nina conditions. Published 2026-03-23.

Our reading, flagged so nobody records it as a revision. WMO's January consolidated statement gave 1.44 plus or minus 0.13 C and its March report gives about 1.43 C. Same body, ten weeks apart, one hundredth of a degree, inside a band 0.26 C wide. It is a rounding of a still-settling multi-dataset synthesis, not a correction, and it is a good demonstration of why a figure at this precision needs its uncertainty carried alongside it.

Ocean heat and chemistry: around 29 per cent of the CO2 from human activities between 2015 and 2024 was absorbed by the ocean, and global average ocean surface pH has declined over the past 41 years, with the largest regional decreases in the Indian Ocean, the Southern Ocean, the eastern equatorial Pacific and the northern tropical Pacific. The IPCC holds with very high confidence that present-day surface pH values are unprecedented for at least 26,000 years. Despite La Nina, around 90 per cent of the ocean surface experienced at least one marine heatwave in 2025. Published 2026-03-23.

blocks.caption: NOAA NCEI ocean heat content, 0-2000 m, anomaly against 1955-2006. The 2025 point is the record WMO reports, and it is the input to the derived imbalance above.

blocks.text: Sea level: in 2025 global mean sea level was comparable to the record-high levels of 2024, around 11 cm above the start of the satellite altimetry record in 1993. The year-to-year increase from 2024 to 2025 was smaller than from 2023 to 2024, consistent with short-term variability under La Nina. The rate of rise since 2012 is higher than the rate over the earlier part of the satellite record, 1993-2011. Published 2026-03-23.

Sea ice: the annual average Arctic sea ice extent for 2025 was the lowest or second lowest on record in the satellite era beginning 1979, and the 2025 maximum daily extent after the winter freeze was the lowest annual maximum in the observed record at about 14.19 million km2. Annual average Antarctic extent was the third lowest, after 2023 and 2024, and the annual minimum daily extent tied for the second lowest, with the four lowest Antarctic minima all falling in the past four years. Published 2026-03-23.

Glaciers: in the 2024/2025 hydrological year, mass loss from the reference glaciers was among the five worst on record. Eight of the ten years with the largest glacier ice loss have occurred since 2016. Exceptional loss occurred in Iceland and along the Pacific coast of North America in 2025. Published 2026-03-23.

Greenhouse gases: levels of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide continued to increase in 2025 at individual monitoring stations. In 2024, the last year with consolidated global observations, atmospheric CO2 reached its highest level in the last 2 million years and methane and nitrous oxide their highest in at least the last 800,000 years. The annual CO2 increase in 2024 was the largest since modern measurements began in 1957, which WMO attributes to continued fossil CO2 emissions and reduced effectiveness of the land and ocean carbon sinks. Published 2026-03-23.

The report is accompanied by an interactive story map, a supplement on extreme events assembled with IOM, IDMC, UNHCR, WFP and FAO, and a chapter on climate and health covering dengue and heat stress. Those are outside what this round checked.

Our closing reading. Adding the energy imbalance to the indicator list changes what the annual report is for. A list of surface temperature, sea level, sea ice, glaciers and ocean pH is a list of consequences, each with its own lag and its own noise. The imbalance is the input to all of them, and it is the one quantity that answers the blunt question directly: is the planet still accumulating energy, and faster or slower than before. It is also the indicator most likely to move first if anything ever changes, which makes it the one worth watching even in a year when the temperature ranking is dull.

knowledge: Earth's energy imbalance recorded as a WMO headline indicator for the first time, with the excess-energy partition (ocean above 91 per cent, land about 5, ice about 3, atmosphere about 1) and the 2005-2025 ocean uptake rate of 11.0 to 12.2 ZJ per year. Plus a checked cross-comparison of this project's derived imbalance series against that WMO figure: our 10-year window ending 2025 implies 11.4 ZJ per year and a full 2005-2025 straight-line fit implies 10.83 ZJ per year, computed 2026-08-09.
